title: Peppermint
subtitle: The cooling kitchen herb that doubles as a digestive and pain-relieving remedy
excerpt: Peppermint is the most-used culinary herb that also carries a well-established medicinal reputation. Traditionally taken after meals for indigestion, bloating, and wind, it works through the cooling and antispasmodic action of its volatile oils. A jar of dried leaves keeps a year in the cupboard.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), peppermint entry, Botanical.com transcription. EMA HMPC monograph on Mentha x piperita folium (2008, revised 2020), dosing and paediatric reference. Culpeper's Complete Herbal (1653), mint entry, public domain. British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (1983), peppermint section.

glossaryTerms.definition: The aromatic fraction of a plant that evaporates readily. In peppermint this is the menthol-rich oil responsible for the cooling and antispasmodic effects. Lost from an uncovered cup of tea, which is why the lid matters.
An action that reduces muscle spasm. In the digestive context this means easing the cramping and over-contraction associated with indigestion and irritable bowel.

content.text: Peppermint in the home kitchen is the dried leaf steeped into a pale green cup of tea, the cooling breath after a heavy meal, the herb that has worked its way into every corner of the food and remedy cupboard. It is the most-used culinary herb that also carries a serious medicinal reputation. Western herbalists have relied on it for digestive complaints for centuries: trapped wind, indigestion, nausea, and the cramping gut. A jar of dried peppermint leaves keeps a year in the cupboard and makes a reliable everyday cup.
Precautions
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Paediatric caution: concentrated peppermint oil should never be applied to the face, chest, or nostrils of infants and young children. The menthol vapour can cause a slowing of breathing in babies. This does not apply to a weak peppermint tea at culinary strength, which is tolerated from school age upward, but menthol rubs and neat peppermint oil are not for small children. If you are considering any peppermint preparation for a child under twelve, consult a herbalist who specialises in children's herbal medicine or a paediatric doctor first.

Reflux: peppermint relaxes the muscle at the lower end of the oesophagus, which is useful for digestion but can worsen symptoms in readers with significant acid reflux or hiatus hernia. If peppermint tea reliably makes reflux worse, it is not the right herb for your digestion.
Botanical

Mentha x piperita, family Lamiaceae. Peppermint is a hybrid: a cross between watermint and spearmint that arose naturally and has been cultivated ever since. The x in the binomial marks the hybrid origin. Parts used are the leaf and the whole aerial parts harvested just before flowering when the
volatile oil

content is highest. Because it is a hybrid it does not breed true from seed; it spreads by runners and is best grown from a cutting or bought as a plant. It grows vigorously in a pot or open ground in full sun to partial shade and will take over a border if not contained.
active compounds and actions

The main oil in peppermint is menthol, with menthone as a secondary compound. Menthol activates cold-sensitive receptors in the skin and mucous membranes without lowering the actual temperature. This cooling action is behind peppermint's use for headaches applied to the temples and the familiar sensation from peppermint tea steam.
The
antispasmodic

action is the one that gives peppermint its digestive reputation. Menthol relaxes smooth muscle in the gut wall, easing cramping and allowing trapped gas to move. This is the same mechanism behind the use of peppermint oil capsules for irritable bowel symptoms: limited clinical-trial evidence supports the traditional use for cramping gut and bloating. The wind-easing action (easing of wind) follows naturally from the eases muscle spasm effect on the gut.
Traditional uses

Western herbal and folk European traditions use peppermint mainly as a digestive herb. The main uses are indigestion after a heavy meal, trapped wind, nausea, and the cramping of an irritable gut. Peppermint tea is one of the oldest after-dinner remedies. It is also used as a diluted oil applied to the temples for tension headaches.

The cooling and antimicrobial properties of the oil make peppermint a traditional gargle for sore mouths. As a steam inhalation, a handful of dried peppermint in just-boiled water is used for head colds. The menthol creates a sensation of easier breathing and may ease discomfort during acute colds.
Preparations

The standard preparation is a hot infusion: one heaped teaspoon of dried leaves per cup, covered with just-off-boil water, steeped covered for eight to ten minutes. Covering the cup is important because the volatile oil is the active fraction and it evaporates readily from an uncovered cup. Strain before drinking. Fresh leaves make a pleasant drink but are less concentrated than dried.

For topical use on the temples for a tension headache, a few drops of diluted peppermint essential oil (never neat) applied with the fingertips is the traditional preparation. A compress of cooled strong peppermint tea applied to the forehead is a gentler alternative. Neither of these preparations is appropriate for young children (see the safety notes above).
Cautions and cautions

Paediatric caution: concentrated peppermint oil should never be applied to the face or chest of infants and small children. The menthol vapour carries a risk of slowing breathing in babies. This caution applies to menthol rubs and neat peppermint oil, not to a weak tea at culinary strength. Consult a paediatric herbalist or doctor before using any peppermint preparation in children under twelve.

Acid reflux and hiatus hernia: the same muscle-relaxing action that eases the gut can allow stomach acid to rise into the oesophagus. Readers with significant reflux or a hiatus hernia often find peppermint makes their symptoms worse. If this applies to you, choose a different digestive herb such as chamomile or fennel.

Drug interactions: no notable interactions have been found at culinary tea doses. High-dose peppermint oil capsules may affect how the liver processes some medicines. Readers on regular medication who use high-dose peppermint oil capsules should check with their prescriber.
